artboards.title: Option B — Search first, facets behind pickers
Option C — One dense list, top-N everywhere

annotations.text:
YASTL sidebar

All three directions drop the Collections cover thumbnails and colour dots. The audit found that split is not a styling choice: a collection gets a thumbnail only when it still has leftover rows in collection_models, and a dot when it does not. 'Garage' is a smart collection with 338 matches and zero manual rows, so it gets a dot; 'Art' has two stale manual rows and takes its cover from one of them. The marker encodes nothing a reader can use, and it shifts the name's left edge by 10px from row to row.

The bigger finding: the sidebar's problem is mostly its DATA, not its layout. Numbers on each board.

260px wide, 908px tall collapsed, 5,231px with all three sections open — 5.8 screenfuls.

Only 23% of the column is text; the rest is padding from 44px touch-target floors applied unconditionally at desktop.

30 of the 30 tags shown by default are punctuation fragments. The auto-tagger never strips punctuation and still runs on every scan, so this regenerates.

30 of 53 category counts disagree with what clicking returns — one says 6 and returns 272.

Least change. Same five sections, same mental model.

Ornaments gone. Rows 44px -> 32px on desktop. Formats come from the live histogram, so the five that match zero models disappear. Tags lead with most-used instead of alphabetical, which is what buries the junk. Categories show the top few with a 'browse all' escape.

Cheapest to build, and it fixes the two things you can see. Does not fix the junk tags or the wrong counts at source.

Search is the primary control; the endless lists move behind pickers that open on demand.

Adds a 'Filtering by' block — the app currently never shows you what is applied in one place, and on mobile choosing a filter does not even close the drawer.

Best fit for a library this size: 1,605 tags and 756 categories are never going to be a browsable list. Most work, and the pickers are new UI.

No sections that collapse, no trees, no pickers — one flat 28px-row list showing the top of each facet with a link out.

Fits everything above the fold on a laptop, which nothing else here does.

Weakest for power use: if you want a tag outside the top five you must go to a separate screen. Best if you mostly re-visit the same handful of collections.

None of these three fixes the data, and the data is the real problem:

• 1,605 tags, of which 451 contain a stray bracket and 519 apply to one model. The default view is 100% junk because it sorts alphabetically and '(' sorts first.
• 756 categories, 99 of them unreachable because the sidebar hand-unrolls exactly three levels. 'files' exists as 59 separate categories, so clicking a chess set returns pegboard brackets.
• Category counts are computed on direct links but filtering rolls up descendants, so 30 of 53 root rows are wrong by up to 272x.

Those are backend fixes, separate from whichever layout you pick. Worth doing first if you want the sidebar to be useful rather than just tidier.
